terms.latin: ut (+ subjunctive), after ita, sīc, tam, adeō, tantus, tālis
terms.grammar: conjunction, with the subjunctive; negative ut nōn
evidence: Sen. Ep. 57.1: tantum lutī tōtā viā fuit ut possim vidērī nihilōminus nāvigāsse
Liv. 21.56.7: ita torpentēs gelū in castra rediēre ut vix laetitiam victōriae sentīrent
terms.comment: The main clause usually has the pointer word (ita, sīc, tam, adeō, tantus, tālis). Unlike purpose, the negative is ut nōn, and the tense may break the sequence to state a plain past fact (ut … prōdiderit).

terms.grammar: conjunction, with the subjunctive, after a negative main clause
evidence: Ter. Haut. 675: Nihil tam difficile est quīn quaerendō investīgārī possiet.
terms.comment: “Nothing is so hard that it cannot …”: quīn = ut nōn after a negative.

phrases.latin: tantum lutī tōtā viā fuit ut possim vidērī nihilōminus nāvigāsse
phrases.english: there was so much mud the whole way that I might as well have gone by sea

phrases.latin: nōs enim ita philologī sumus ut vel cum fabrīs habitāre possīmus
phrases.english: for we are such bookworms that we could even live with the builders in

phrases.latin: ita torpentēs gelū in castra rediēre ut vix laetitiam victōriae sentīrent
phrases.english: they came back to camp so numb with cold that they could hardly feel the joy of victory

phrases.latin: nōn tamen adeō virtūtum sterile saeculum ut nōn et bona exempla prōdiderit
phrases.english: yet the age was not so barren of virtue that it produced no good examples

phrases.latin: Nihil tam difficile est quīn quaerendō investīgārī possiet.
phrases.english: Nothing is so hard that it can’t be found out by searching.
